title: Fourier series; cosine & sine series
summary: Fourier series expand a periodic function in the orthogonal functions 1, cos(nπx/L), sin(nπx/L), with coefficients given by projection integrals. Symmetry halves the work, the convergence theorem says jumps go to the average, and half-range cosine/sine series handle functions given on [0, L].

blocks.text: Fourier series write a periodic function as a sum of sines and cosines. The key is that these functions are orthogonal for the inner product ⟨f, g⟩ = ∫₋ₗᴸ f(x)g(x) dx on C[−L, L], just like an orthogonal basis of ℝⁿ.

blocks.name: Orthogonality integrals
blocks.text: For integers m, n ≥ 1 on [−L, L]: ∫ cos(mπx/L)cos(nπx/L) dx = 0 if m ≠ n and L if m = n; ∫ sin(mπx/L)sin(nπx/L) dx = 0 if m ≠ n and L if m = n; ∫ sin(mπx/L)cos(nπx/L) dx = 0 always; ∫ 1·cos = ∫ 1·sin = 0; ∫ 1·1 = 2L.

proof.text: Product-to-sum: cos A cos B = ½[cos(A − B) + cos(A + B)], sin A sin B = ½[cos(A − B) − cos(A + B)]. For m ≠ n both are cosines of nonzero multiples of πx/L, which integrate to 0 over a full period. For m = n one term is ½·1, giving L. sin·cos is an odd function, so its integral over [−L, L] is 0.

blocks.title: Orthogonality integrals
blocks.prompt: Compute ∫₋π^π sin 2x sin 3x dx, ∫₋π^π cos² 3x dx, ∫₋π^π sin x cos 4x dx and ∫₋₃³ cos(2πx/3)cos(πx/3) dx.
steps: sin 2x sin 3x: different frequencies, L = π ⇒ 0.
cos² 3x: same frequency ⇒ L = π.
sin x cos 4x: sin·cos is odd ⇒ 0.

blocks.text: Fast trick: ∫₋π^π (3 + 2 cos 2x − sin 5x)² dx = 3²·2π + 2²·π + 1²·π = 23π, because all cross terms vanish.
For f on (−L, L) (extended with period 2L): f(x) ~ a₀/2 + Σₙ₌₁^∞ [aₙ cos(nπx/L) + bₙ sin(nπx/L)], with aₙ = (1/L)∫₋ₗᴸ f(x) cos(nπx/L) dx (n ≥ 0) and bₙ = (1/L)∫₋ₗᴸ f(x) sin(nπx/L) dx.

blocks.name: Where the formulas come from
blocks.text: Multiply the series by cos(mπx/L) and integrate over [−L, L]. Orthogonality kills every term except aₘ·L, so aₘ = (1/L)∫ f cos(mπx/L). Same for bₘ.

proof.text: This is exactly the projection coefficient ⟨f, φ⟩/⟨φ, φ⟩ for an orthogonal basis; ⟨φ, φ⟩ = L for each sine/cosine. For the constant 1, ⟨1, 1⟩ = 2L, which is why the constant term is a₀/2 = average value of f.

blocks.text: Useful values: sin nπ = 0, cos nπ = (−1)ⁿ; ∫₀ᴸ x cos(nπx/L) dx = L²((−1)ⁿ − 1)/(nπ)²; ∫₀ᴸ x sin(nπx/L) dx = L²(−1)ⁿ⁺¹/(nπ); ∫₀ᴸ sin(nπx/L) dx = L(1 − (−1)ⁿ)/(nπ).

blocks.title: Fourier series of a piecewise function
blocks.prompt: Find the Fourier series of f(x) = 0 for −2 < x < 0 and f(x) = x for 0 < x < 2 (period 4).
steps: L = 2. a₀ = (1/2)∫₀² x dx = (1/2)(2) = 1, so the constant term is a₀/2 = 1/2.
aₙ = (1/2)∫₀² x cos(nπx/2) dx = (1/2)·4((−1)ⁿ − 1)/(nπ)² = 2((−1)ⁿ − 1)/(n²π²): −4/(n²π²) for odd n, 0 for even n.
f ~ 1/2 − (4/π²)Σ<sub>n odd</sub> cos(nπx/2)/n² + (2/π)Σ (−1)ⁿ⁺¹ sin(nπx/2)/n.

blocks.text: Two classic slips: forgetting the ½ on a₀ (compute a₀ separately, since the aₙ formula often has n in a denominator), and using nx instead of nπx/L when L ≠ π.
Even: f(−x) = f(x) (x², cos, |x|). Odd: f(−x) = −f(x) (x, x³, sin). even·even = odd·odd = even; even·odd = odd. ∫₋ₗᴸ odd = 0; ∫₋ₗᴸ even = 2∫₀ᴸ.

blocks.name: Symmetry kills half the coefficients
blocks.text: If f is even, every bₙ = 0 and aₙ = (2/L)∫₀ᴸ f cos(nπx/L): a cosine series. If f is odd, every aₙ = 0 (including a₀) and bₙ = (2/L)∫₀ᴸ f sin(nπx/L): a sine series.

proof.text: For even f, f(x) sin(nπx/L) is even·odd = odd, so its integral over [−L, L] is 0, while f cos is even, so ∫₋ₗᴸ = 2∫₀ᴸ. The odd case is symmetric. Intuitively: sines are odd, so they cannot help build an even function.

blocks.title: Use symmetry: x² on (−π, π)
blocks.prompt: Find the Fourier series of f(x) = x² on (−π, π).
steps: x² is even ⇒ bₙ = 0.
a₀ = (2/π)∫₀^π x² dx = 2π²/3 ⇒ constant term π²/3.
aₙ = (2/π)∫₀^π x² cos nx dx = 4(−1)ⁿ/n² (integrate by parts twice).
x² ~ π²/3 + 4Σ (−1)ⁿ cos nx / n² = π²/3 − 4cos x + cos 2x − (4/9)cos 3x + ⋯.

blocks.text: Split a function into even and odd parts when it is a sum: x + x² on (−1, 1) has its cosine terms from x² and its sine terms from x.

lesson.title: Convergence: what the series equals, including jumps

blocks.name: Fourier convergence theorem
blocks.text: If f and f′ are piecewise continuous on [−L, L], the Fourier series converges at every x to ½[f(x⁺) + f(x⁻)] for the 2L-periodic extension of f. So it equals f(x) where the extension is continuous, and the average of the one-sided limits at a jump. At x = ±L it converges to ½[f(−L⁺) + f(L⁻)].

Why the average: every partial sum is a smooth function, and the symmetric pull of the two sides of a jump balances at the midpoint. Changing f at a single point changes no integral, so the series cannot 'know' f(c) at a jump anyway.

blocks.title: What does the series converge to at x = c?
items: Reduce c by multiples of 2L into (−L, L].
If c is interior and f is continuous there, the answer is f(c).
At a jump, average the left and right limits.
At c = ±L, average f(L⁻) and f(−L⁺) (wrap around).

blocks.title: Values at jumps and endpoints
blocks.prompt: For f = 0 on (−2, 0), f = x on (0, 2), period 4: to what does the series converge at x = 0, 1, 2, −1, 5, 6?
steps: x = 1: continuous, f(1) = 1.
x = −1: continuous, 0.

lesson.title: Cosine and sine series on [0, L]

blocks.text: A function given only on (0, L) can be extended to (−L, L) in two natural ways, then periodically with period 2L.

blocks.name: Half-range expansions
blocks.text: Even extension ⇒ Fourier cosine series f ~ a₀/2 + Σ aₙ cos(nπx/L), aₙ = (2/L)∫₀ᴸ f cos(nπx/L) dx. Odd extension ⇒ Fourier sine series f ~ Σ bₙ sin(nπx/L), bₙ = (2/L)∫₀ᴸ f sin(nπx/L) dx.

proof.text: Apply the even/odd symmetry theorem to the extended function on (−L, L).

items: The cosine series (even extension) has no jump at x = 0 or x = L from the extension itself, so it converges to f(0⁺) and f(L⁻) there.
The sine series is 0 at x = 0 and x = L (every term vanishes), whatever f is: it converges to the average of f(0⁺) and −f(0⁺).

blocks.title: Cosine and sine series of x on [0, π]
blocks.prompt: Find the cosine series and the sine series of f(x) = x on (0, π). What does each converge to at x = π?
steps: Cosine: a₀ = (2/π)∫₀^π x dx = π ⇒ constant π/2. aₙ = (2/π)∫₀^π x cos nx dx = 2((−1)ⁿ − 1)/(πn²): −4/(πn²) for odd n.
x ~ π/2 − (4/π)[cos x + cos 3x/9 + cos 5x/25 + ⋯] (even extension = |x|, continuous).
Sine: bₙ = (2/π)∫₀^π x sin nx dx = 2(−1)ⁿ⁺¹/n.
x ~ 2[sin x − sin 2x/2 + sin 3x/3 − ⋯] (odd extension = sawtooth).
At x = π: cosine series → π (the even extension is continuous there); sine series → 0 (the odd extension jumps from π to −π).
blocks.answer: Cosine: π/2 + Σ 2((−1)ⁿ − 1)/(πn²) cos nx; sine: Σ 2(−1)ⁿ⁺¹ sin(nx)/n; at x = π: π and 0

blocks.text: Half-range coefficients use 2/L and ∫₀ᴸ; full-range coefficients use 1/L and ∫₋ₗᴸ. Mixing them doubles or halves every coefficient.

blocks.title: Recipe
items: Find the Fourier series of a suitable f.
Pick a point x₀ where the cos/sin values are simple (0, L, L/2) and you know the series' value (f(x₀) if continuous, the average if a jump).
Set the two equal and solve for the numerical sum.

blocks.title: Σ 1/n² and Σ(−1)ⁿ⁺¹/n² from x²
blocks.prompt: Using x² ~ π²/3 + Σ 4(−1)ⁿ cos(nx)/n² on (−π, π), evaluate Σ 1/n² and Σ (−1)ⁿ⁺¹/n².
steps: At x = π the periodic extension of x² is continuous (π² from both sides), so the series equals π².

blocks.title: Σ over odd n from the cosine series of x
blocks.prompt: Use the cosine series of x on (0, π) to find 1 + 1/3² + 1/5² + ⋯.
steps: x ~ π/2 − (4/π)Σ<sub>odd</sub> cos nx/n², valid at x = 0 (continuous even extension, value 0).
0 = π/2 − (4/π)Σ<sub>odd</sub> 1/n² ⇒ Σ<sub>odd</sub> 1/n² = π²/8.

blocks.title: True/False
blocks.prompt: (a) The Fourier series of a piecewise smooth f converges to f(x) everywhere. (b) An odd function's series has only sine terms. (c) The sine series of f on (0, L) converges at 0 to f(0⁺). (d) {1, cos x, sin x, cos 2x, …} is orthogonal on [0, π]. (e) sin 3x + 2 cos 5x is its own Fourier series on [−π, π].
steps: (a) False: at jumps it gives the average.
(b) True: f cos is odd, so every aₙ = 0.
(c) False: it converges to 0.
(d) False: ∫₀^π sin x dx = 2 ≠ 0; orthogonality needs a full period.
(e) True: b₃ = 1, a₅ = 2, all other coefficients 0 by orthogonality.

cards.front: Why are 1, cos(nπx/L), sin(nπx/L) orthogonal on [−L, L]? State the integrals.

back.text: ∫ cos(mπx/L)cos(nπx/L) = ∫ sin·sin = 0 (m ≠ n), L (m = n ≥ 1); ∫ sin·cos = 0
Inner product ⟨f, g⟩ = ∫₋ₗᴸ f g dx; also ∫ 1·1 = 2L.
Why: Product-to-sum gives cosines of (m ± n)πx/L, which integrate to 0 over full periods; sin·cos is odd.

cards.front: Fourier series on [−L, L]: the series and the coefficient formulas.

back.text: f ~ a₀/2 + Σ [aₙcos(nπx/L) + bₙsin(nπx/L)]
aₙ = (1/L)∫₋ₗᴸ f cos(nπx/L) dx,   bₙ = (1/L)∫₋ₗᴸ f sin(nπx/L) dx
a₀/2 = average value of f.
Forgetting the ½ on a₀; compute a₀ separately (the aₙ formula often has n in a denominator).

cards.front: Where do the coefficient formulas come from?

back.text: Multiply the series by cos(mπx/L) and integrate over [−L, L]. Orthogonality kills every term except aₘ·L.
∫ f cos(mπx/L) dx = aₘL
It’s exactly the projection coefficient ⟨f, φ⟩/⟨φ, φ⟩ for an orthogonal basis (Lay 6.7).

cards.front: Fourier series of f = 0 on (−2, 0), f = 3 on (0, 2).

back.title: Steps
items: L = 2. a₀ = ½∫₀² 3 dx = 3 (constant term 3/2).
aₙ = ½∫₀² 3cos(nπx/2) dx = 0.
bₙ = ½∫₀² 3sin(nπx/2) dx = 3(1 − (−1)ⁿ)/(nπ): 6/(nπ) for odd n.

back.text: Example: f ~ 3/2 + (6/π)[sin(πx/2) + ⅓sin(3πx/2) + ⋯].

cards.front: Useful values and integrals for Fourier computations.

items: sin nπ = 0, cos nπ = (−1)ⁿ.
∫₀ᴸ x cos(nπx/L) dx = L²((−1)ⁿ − 1)/(nπ)².
∫₀ᴸ x sin(nπx/L) dx = L²(−1)ⁿ⁺¹/(nπ).
∫₀ᴸ sin(nπx/L) dx = L(1 − (−1)ⁿ)/(nπ).

cards.front: Fourier series of f(x) = x + x² on [−1, 1].

back.title: Steps
items: Split: x² even (cosines), x odd (sines).
a₀ = ∫₋₁¹ x² dx = 2/3 (constant 1/3).
aₙ = ∫₋₁¹ x²cos nπx dx = 4(−1)ⁿ/(n²π²).
bₙ = 2∫₀¹ x sin nπx dx = 2(−1)ⁿ⁺¹/(nπ).

back.text: Example: f ~ 1/3 + Σ[4(−1)ⁿ/(n²π²) cos nπx + 2(−1)ⁿ⁺¹/(nπ) sin nπx].

cards.front: What does a Fourier series converge to? State the theorem.

back.text: If f and f′ are piecewise continuous on [−L, L], the series converges at every x to
of the 2L-periodic extension. At x = ±L: ½[f(−L⁺) + f(L⁻)].
The value f(c) at a jump is irrelevant: changing one point doesn’t change any integral.

cards.front: Recipe: what does the series converge to at x = c?

back.title: Steps
items: Shift c by multiples of 2L into (−L, L].
If f is continuous there (not an endpoint), the answer is f(c).
At a jump or at ±L, average the left and right limits.

cards.front: Even and odd functions: definitions, product rules, integrals.

items: Even: f(−x) = f(x) (x², cos, |x|). Odd: f(−x) = −f(x) (x, x³, sin).
even·even = odd·odd = even; even·odd = odd.
∫₋ₗᴸ odd = 0; ∫₋ₗᴸ even = 2∫₀ᴸ.

back.text: f even ⇒ bₙ = 0; f odd ⇒ aₙ = 0

cards.front: Fourier cosine and sine series of f on [0, L]: what extension, what formulas?

back.text: cosine: aₙ = (2/L)∫₀ᴸ f cos(nπx/L)   (even extension)
sine: bₙ = (2/L)∫₀ᴸ f sin(nπx/L)   (odd extension)
Both have period 2L. The sine series is always 0 at x = 0 and x = L.
Half-range uses 2/L and ∫₀ᴸ; full series uses 1/L and ∫₋ₗᴸ.

cards.front: Cosine and sine series of f(x) = 2 − x on [0, 2]. Values at x = 0?

back.title: Steps
items: Cosine: a₀ = 2, aₙ = 4(1 − (−1)ⁿ)/(n²π²): 1 + (8/π²)Σ_odd cos(nπx/2)/n².
Sine: bₙ = 4/(nπ): Σ (4/(nπ)) sin(nπx/2).

back.text: Example: At x = 0: cosine series → 2 (even extension is continuous); sine series → 0 (odd extension jumps from −2 to 2).

cards.front: Square wave f = −1 on (−π, 0), 1 on (0, π): series and value at x = π.

back.title: Steps
items: Odd, so aₙ = 0.
bₙ = (2/π)∫₀^π sin nx dx = 2(1 − (−1)ⁿ)/(nπ).
f ~ (4/π)[sin x + ⅓sin 3x + ⅕sin 5x + ⋯].

cards.front: Fourier sine series of f(x) = x on [0, 1].

back.title: Steps
items: L = 1: bₙ = 2∫₀¹ x sin nπx dx.

back.text: Example: x ~ Σ 2(−1)ⁿ⁺¹ sin(nπx)/(nπ) on (0, 1); at x = 1 it gives 0 (odd extension jumps from 1 to −1).

cards.front: Fourier series of x² on [−3, 3]; and of sin 3x + 2cos 5x on [−π, π].

back.title: Steps
items: x² is even: a₀ = (2/3)∫₀³ x² dx = 6; aₙ = 36(−1)ⁿ/(n²π²).
x² ~ 3 + Σ 36(−1)ⁿ/(n²π²) cos(nπx/3).

back.text: Example: sin 3x + 2cos 5x is already its own Fourier series: b₃ = 1, a₅ = 2, all else 0 (orthogonality).

cards.front: Why does an even function have only cosine terms?

back.text: f(x)sin(nπx/L) is even·odd = odd, so every bₙ = (1/L)∫₋ₗᴸ f sin = 0. Sines are odd and cannot build an even function.

cards.front: What does a Fourier series converge to at a jump discontinuity?

back.text: The average ½[f(x⁺) + f(x⁻)] of the one-sided limits (of the periodic extension).
x² ~ π²/3 + Σ4(−1)ⁿcos(nx)/n² on (−π, π); at x = π: π² = π²/3 + 4Σ1/n² ⇒ π²/6.

cards.front: ∫₋π^π cos² nx dx, ∫₋π^π sin² nx dx, ∫₋π^π 1 dx?

hard.title: Full Fourier series and Σ 1/(odd)²

prompt.text: Convention: on (−L, L), f ~ a₀/2 + Σ[aₙ cos(nπx/L) + bₙ sin(nπx/L)] with aₙ = (1/L)∫f cos, bₙ = (1/L)∫f sin.
Find the Fourier series of f(x) = 0 for −π < x < 0, f(x) = x for 0 < x < π (period 2π). What does it converge to at x = 0 and x = π? Use x = π to evaluate 1 + 1/3² + 1/5² + ⋯.

hard.answer: f ~ π/4 + Σ[((−1)ⁿ − 1)/(πn²) cos nx + (−1)ⁿ⁺¹ sin(nx)/n]; converges to 0 at x = 0 and π/2 at x = π; Σ_odd 1/n² = π²/8

solution.title: Solution
items: a₀ = (1/π)∫₀^π x dx = π/2, so the constant term is π/4.
aₙ = (1/π)∫₀^π x cos nx dx = (1/π)[x sin nx/n + cos nx/n²]₀^π = ((−1)ⁿ − 1)/(πn²): −2/(πn²) for odd n, 0 for even.
f ~ π/4 − (2/π)Σodd n cos nx/n² + Σ (−1)ⁿ⁺¹ sin nx/n.
x = 0: f continuous there ⇒ 0. x = π: jump from π (left) to 0 (right, by periodicity) ⇒ π/2.
At x = π: π/2 = π/4 − (2/π)Σodd (cos nπ)/n² = π/4 + (2/π)Σodd 1/n² ⇒ Σodd 1/n² = π²/8.

solution.text: What it tests: The series at a jump converges to the midpoint — and that midpoint value is exactly what makes the series identity come out right.

hard.title: Even pulse of period 4; Leibniz series

prompt.text: Let f on (−2, 2) be 1 for |x| < 1 and 0 for 1 < |x| < 2, extended with period 4. Find its Fourier series and the value it converges to at x = 1. Then use x = 0 to sum 1 − 1/3 + 1/5 − ⋯.

solution.title: Solution
items: f is even ⇒ bₙ = 0. L = 2.

solution.text: What it tests: With period 2L = 4, the frequencies are nπx/2, not nx. Using symmetry halves the integrals.

hard.title: Cosine vs sine series of cos x

prompt.text: Let f(x) = cos x on (0, π). (a) What is its cosine series? (b) Find its sine series. (c) To what does the sine series converge at x = 0, π/2, π?

hard.answer: (a) cos x (b) bₙ = 4n/(π(n² − 1)) for even n, 0 for odd n (c) 0, 0, 0

solution.title: Solution
items: (a) cos x is already one of the cosine basis functions: the cosine series is just cos x (a₁ = 1, all others 0).
(b) bₙ = (2/π)∫₀^π cos x sin nx dx. Use sin nx cos x = ½[sin(n+1)x + sin(n−1)x].
cos x ~ (8/π)Σk≥1 k sin 2kx/(4k² − 1).
(c) x = π/2: f continuous ⇒ cos(π/2) = 0. x = 0 and π: the odd extension jumps between ±1 ⇒ 0 at both — not f(0⁺) = 1.

solution.text: What it tests: The cosine series of a function already in the basis is itself — no integration. The sine series of the same function looks nothing like it.

items: 1. The Fourier series of a piecewise smooth 2L-periodic f converges to f(x) at every x.
2. The Fourier series of an odd function contains only sine terms.
3. The cosine series of f on (0, L) converges at x = 0 to f(0⁺).
4. The sine series of f on (0, L) converges at x = 0 to f(0⁺).
5. The product of two odd functions is odd.
6. {1, cos x, sin x, cos 2x, sin 2x, …} is orthogonal on [0, π].
1. False. At a jump it converges to the average ½[f(x⁺) + f(x⁻)].
2. True. f(x) cos(nπx/L) is odd, so every aₙ (including a₀) integrates to 0.
3. True. The even extension has matching one-sided limits f(0⁺) on both sides of 0.
4. False. Every sine term is 0 at x = 0, so it converges to 0 (the average of f(0⁺) and −f(0⁺)).
5. False. (−f)(−g) = fg: even. E.g. x·sin x.
6. False. ∫₀^π 1·sin x dx = 2 ≠ 0. Orthogonal on a full period [−π, π].

solution.text: What it tests: Even extension → cosine series, continuous at the ends. Odd extension → sine series, forced to 0 at 0 and L.

prompt.text: (a) Compute ∫₋π^π (3 + 2 cos 2x − sin 5x)² dx without expanding everything. (b) Find the Fourier series of sin³x on (−π, π) without integrating.

solution.title: Solution
items: (a) Cross terms integrate to 0 (orthogonality). ∫ 3² = 18π, ∫ (2 cos 2x)² = 4π, ∫ sin² 5x = π. Total 23π.
(b) sin³x = sin x·(1 − cos 2x)/2 = ½ sin x − ¼[sin 3x − sin x] = (3/4) sin x − (1/4) sin 3x. A finite trig sum is its own Fourier series.

solution.text: What it tests: ∫₋π^π cos² nx = ∫ sin² nx = π (n ≥ 1), ∫ 1² = 2π. This is the inner-product picture applied to trig functions.

hard.title: Convergence values at jumps and endpoints

prompt.text: f on (−2, 2) is x² for −2 < x < 0, 3 for 0 < x < 1, 1 − x for 1 < x < 2, extended with period 4. To what does its Fourier series converge at x = 0, 1, 2, −1, ½, 5, 7?

solution.title: Solution
items: x = 2: left limit 1 − 2 = −1; right limit = f(−2⁺) = 4 (periodicity). ½(−1 + 4) = 3/2.
x = −1: continuous, 1. x = ½: 3.

solution.text: What it tests: At the endpoints ±L, pair the left limit at L with the right limit at −L. Reduce other x mod 2L first.

hard.title: Construct: convergence to f and failure

prompt.text: (a) Give a function on (−π, π) whose Fourier series converges at x = 0 to a value different from f(0). (b) Give a nonzero continuous f on [0, π] whose sine series converges to f at every point of [0, π], and explain.

hard.answer: (a) e.g. 0 for x < 0, 1 for x ≥ 0 (series gives ½ at 0) (b) e.g. f(x) = x(π − x)

solution.title: Solution
items: (a) f(x) = 0 for x < 0, 1 for x ≥ 0: f(0) = 1, but the series gives ½.
(b) Need the odd periodic extension to be continuous: requires f(0) = 0 and f(π) = 0. E.g. f(x) = x(π − x) (piecewise smooth, continuous extension ⇒ convergence everywhere).

solution.text: What it tests: Pointwise convergence to f needs continuity of the extension, not just of f on the open interval.

hard.title: Sine series of x(π − x); Σ ±1/(odd)³

prompt.text: Find the sine series of f(x) = x(π − x) on (0, π), and evaluate at x = π/2 to find 1 − 1/3³ + 1/5³ − 1/7³ + ⋯.

hard.answer: bₙ = 8/(πn³) for odd n, 0 for even; 1 − 1/3³ + 1/5³ − ⋯ = π³/32

solution.title: Solution
items: bₙ = (2/π)∫₀^π x(π − x) sin nx dx. Integrate by parts twice (boundary terms vanish because f(0) = f(π) = 0): bₙ = (4/(πn³))(1 − (−1)ⁿ).
bₙ = 8/(πn³) for odd n, 0 for even.
Continuous odd extension ⇒ equality at π/2: π²/4 = (8/π)Σodd sin(nπ/2)/n³ = (8/π)(1 − 1/3³ + 1/5³ − ⋯).

solution.text: What it tests: sin(nπ/2) alternates 1, 0, −1, 0, … — that’s where the alternating signs come from.

hard.title: Periodic forcing by a square wave

prompt.text: The odd square wave s(x) = −1 on (−π, 0), 1 on (0, π), period 2π, has series (4/π)Σodd n sin nx/n. (a) Verify one coefficient. (b) Find a 2π-periodic solution of y″ + 2y = s(x) as a series. (c) For which ω > 0 does y″ + ω²y = s(x) have no 2π-periodic solution?

hard.answer: (b) y = (4/π)Σ_odd sin(nx)/(n(2 − n²)) (c) ω an odd integer

solution.title: Solution
items: (b) Try y = ΣBₙ sin nx: y″ + 2y = Σ(2 − n²)Bₙ sin nx. Match: Bₙ = 4/(πn(2 − n²)) for odd n.
y = (4/π)Σodd sin nx/(n(2 − n²)) (never divides by 0 since n² ≠ 2).

(c) The same matching needs ω² − n² ≠ 0 for every odd n present. If ω is an odd integer, the term sin ωx resonates and no periodic solution exists. (Even integers are fine: those modes are absent from s.)

solution.text: What it tests: Termwise undetermined coefficients: each Fourier mode is a forcing term. Resonance happens only with modes actually present in the forcing.

keyFacts: f ~ a₀/2 + Σ[aₙcos(nπx/L) + bₙsin(nπx/L)], aₙ = (1/L)∫₋ₗᴸ f cos(nπx/L), bₙ = (1/L)∫₋ₗᴸ f sin(nπx/L).
Orthogonality on [−L, L]: ∫cos·cos = ∫sin·sin = 0 (m ≠ n), L (m = n); ∫sin·cos = 0; ∫1 = 2L.
Even f: bₙ = 0, aₙ = (2/L)∫₀ᴸ f cos. Odd f: aₙ = 0, bₙ = (2/L)∫₀ᴸ f sin.
Converges to ½[f(x⁺) + f(x⁻)] of the periodic extension; at ±L average f(L⁻) and f(−L⁺).
Half-range: cosine series = even extension, sine series = odd extension (sine series is 0 at 0 and L).
Numerical series: evaluate the Fourier series at a convenient point (Σ1/n² = π²/6, Σ_odd 1/n² = π²/8).
